node.label: François Furet
node.date_label: “Le Catéchisme révolutionnaire” (1971) · Penser la Révolution française (1978) · Interpreting the French Revolution: Elborg Forster translation (1981) · Le Passé d’une illusion (1995)
node.description: A historian of the French Revolution and political ideas whose work challenged an established social interpretation of revolution. In the opening of his 1971 essay he attacks what he calls a Jacobin historiography, distinguishing its commemorative commitments from critical inquiry. Gérard Grunberg’s substantive 1979 reading identifies a further argument about political language and the representation of popular sovereignty. Both the polemic and its later interpretation remain attributed; the entry does not endorse either a general verdict on Marx or an inevitable path from 1789 to twentieth-century regimes.

node.scope_note: New identity matched to the French-Revolution historian and BnF/Académie records. Argument support is the bounded original essay and Grunberg’s expressly named reading. Furet/Richet coauthorship of earlier work remains distinct; no group work is reassigned. Original essay, revised collection, translation and later monograph stay separate. His criticism targets a particular historical interpretation, not a personal causal influence or blanket theory classification.

incident_edges.relationship: Challenges a specific Marxist/Jacobin historiography of the French Revolution for reproducing revolutionary and commemorative categories.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary pp. 255–256 read. Furet’s polemical label and diagnosis remain his claims about a specific historiographical dispute, not a critique of every Marxist or a personal arrow to Marx.

incident_edges.relationship: Examines political language and claims to represent the people as mechanisms of revolutionary power.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Named reader Gérard Grunberg, pp. 895 and 897, on Penser. Full book unread; no universal acceptance, deterministic twentieth-century analogy or inference from institutional membership.

incident_edges.relationship: Ginzburg disputes Furet’s restriction of subordinate-class history to quantitative and anonymous reconstruction, defending individual cases where the evidence permits.
incident_edges.evidence_note: He explicitly names Furet before defending the possibility of reconstructing individual personalities. This is a methodological criticism, not rejection of quantitative history as such or proof of every Menocchio interpretation. Furet’s underlying text was not newly read.

incident_edges.relationship: Corbin criticizes the republic-centered account he associates with Furet for reducing much of nineteenth-century France to steps toward a later republican outcome.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own 2006 answer also names Maurice Agulhon, whose credit is retained here without inventing a standalone endpoint. Corbin argues for studying monarchies, conflicting political emotions and other periods on their own terms. This records his specific historiographical criticism, not a claim that all of Furet’s work is teleological; Furet’s original books remain unread in this dossier.

incident_edges.relationship: Roche recalls contributing his study of booksellers’ classifications to Furet’s book-history inquiry and receiving Furet’s acknowledgment for it.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own retrospective answer15, printed164, specifically identifies Livre et Société and note16 in Furet’s text. The original Furet acknowledgment was not independently read here. This is a recalled research contribution, not an inference from knowing Furet or sole authorship of the inquiry.

verification.note: Selected primary printed pp. xvii–xix read by OCR of the scan; title and copyright pages checked for translators, 1976 original, 1980 English and 1992 Hopkins Paperbacks manifestation. Ginzburg credits attention to exclusions while criticizing the treatment of excluded people and refusal of interpretation. The original Italian, French Foucault works and Pierre Riviere collection were not independently read for this audit; this is Ginzburg’s attributed interpretation. Additional independently checked primary coverage, 2026-10-25: printed xviii–xx visually read for the Derrida/Furet responses; the coordinator also checked the examples/praise paragraphs on xvii and xix for Davis, Thompson and Le Goff. The 1976 Italian preface, 1980 joint Tedeschi English translation and 1992 paperback manifestation remain distinct. The cited scholars’ underlying works were not newly read; neither a whole-book reading nor a general formative debt is inferred.
